solution.concept_anchor: Multi-state vs. single-state cooperative societies
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students associate Amul with cooperative success stories and may know it operates nationally, but may not precisely recall whether it is a multi-state or state-level cooperative.
elimination_logic: IFFCO: registered as a multi-state cooperative society — operates in multiple states for fertiliser procurement and supply. Multi-state.
GCMMF (Amul): operates across India with milk procurement from multiple states — a multi-state cooperative. Multi-state.
Saraswat Cooperative Bank: primarily operates in Maharashtra — a single-state cooperative registered under Maharashtra's cooperative law. Single-state/state-level.
KRIBHCO: multi-state cooperative society in the fertiliser sector, similar to IFFCO. Multi-state.
Saraswat Cooperative Bank is the odd one out — the only single-state cooperative among the four. Answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic scope trap here distinguishes between single-state and multi-state cooperative societies. All four are well-known cooperatives, but Saraswat Cooperative Bank operates primarily within Maharashtra and is governed by state cooperative law. The other three (IFFCO, GCMMF/Amul, KRIBHCO) operate across multiple states and are registered under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act. Students who know all four are 'cooperatives' without tracking their geographic scope will miss this distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
The multi-state vs. single-state distinction in cooperatives has constitutional and regulatory significance — multi-state cooperatives fall under central law, while single-state cooperatives remain under state jurisdiction.

• Option (a) IFFCO: Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative — multi-state cooperative society, operations spanning all major agricultural states. Part of this group.
• Option (b) GCMMF (Amul): Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation — while its origins are in Gujarat, GCMMF/Amul operates nationally and is a multi-state entity for regulatory purposes. Part of this group.
• Option (c) Saraswat Cooperative Bank: Primarily a Maharashtra-based urban cooperative bank, governed under Maharashtra state cooperative laws. This is the single-state cooperative — the odd one out.
• Option (d) KRIBHCO: Krishak Bharati Cooperative Limited — multi-state cooperative in the fertiliser sector. Part of this group.

Value Addition:
• Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act 2002 governs cooperatives operating in two or more states.
• Part IXB (97th Amendment) applies to multi-state cooperatives; single-state remain under State List Entry 32.
• Urban cooperative banks are supervised by both RBI (banking operations) and Registrar of Cooperative Societies.

solution.concept_anchor: VGF — DEA administration; HAM vs. BOT risk allocation

statement_analysis.statement: Viability Gap Funding (VGF) is a government grant provided to make infrastructure projects commercially viable where the expected revenues are insufficient to cover costs; it is administered by the Department of Economic Affairs.
statement_analysis.reason: VGF is a scheme under the DEA and provides upfront capital support (up to 20% of project cost, extendable to 40% with state contribution) to bridge the viability gap in infrastructure PPPs.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) for road projects, the private developer bears both construction risk and traffic/revenue risk throughout the concession period.
statement_analysis.reason: Under HAM, the government bears the revenue/traffic risk because toll collection rights vest with NHAI; the private developer bears only construction and O&M (operations and maintenance) risk.

statement_analysis.statement: In a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT-Toll) PPP arrangement, the private concessionaire earns revenues through toll collection and bears the traffic risk during the concession period.
statement_analysis.reason: BOT-Toll is the model where the developer bears full traffic/revenue risk; revenues come entirely from tolls collected by the developer, with no government annuity payment.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know that HAM was introduced because BOT was risky may assume the developer bears 'both' risks in HAM too, confusing HAM's risk split with BOT's risk allocation.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — VGF administered by DEA, maximum 20% project cost (40% with state support), specifically for commercially unviable infrastructure projects.
Statement 2 is incorrect — HAM shifts revenue/traffic risk to the government (NHAI collects tolls); developer bears only construction and O&M risk.
Statement 3 is correct — BOT-Toll: developer collects tolls, bears full traffic risk, no government annuity.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (d) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the partial-truth trap: HAM was designed precisely because pure BOT placed excessive revenue risk on developers in low-traffic corridors. By stating that the developer bears 'both construction AND revenue risk' in HAM, the statement attributes BOT's risk profile to HAM. A student who knows that HAM involves government payment may still accept this statement thinking that 'the developer takes risks while the government pays' — without distinguishing which specific risk each party bears.
solution.final_explanation:
Risk allocation is the defining feature that distinguishes PPP models from one another.

• Statement 1 — Correct: VGF is a capital grant from the DEA to cover the viability gap in infrastructure projects. It is capped at 20% of total project cost (or 40% when state government contributes). It is distinct from HAM's payment structure.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Under HAM, NHAI retains toll collection rights — meaning revenue/traffic risk rests with the government. The private developer bears construction risk (completing the road on time and to specification) and O&M risk. This is HAM's key advantage over BOT: it removes revenue risk from the developer.
• Statement 3 — Correct: BOT-Toll places all revenue risk on the developer. The private party constructs, collects tolls, operates the highway, and transfers it to the government at concession end. Government makes no payment during the concession period.

Value Addition:
• BOT-Annuity is a hybrid where the developer bears construction risk but receives fixed annuity (no traffic risk) — predates HAM.
• DBFOT (Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer) is a variant giving more design flexibility to the developer.
• NITI Aayog's PPP Appraisal Committee oversees large-value PPP project approvals.

solution.concept_anchor: Disinvestment institutional evolution — DIPAM, NIF, Air India privatisation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students may place the NIF creation after DIPAM's establishment, as both relate to disinvestment proceeds management, without knowing that NIF was created a decade before DIPAM.
elimination_logic: The dedicated Ministry of Disinvestment was created in 1999 under the Vajpayee government — this is the earliest institutional development among the four.
National Investment Fund (NIF) was set up in 2005 by the UPA government to channel disinvestment proceeds.
FIPB abolition occurred in May 2017 — after NIF creation but before Air India privatisation.

Air India's transfer to Tata Sons was completed in January 2022 — the most recent development. Correct sequence: Ministry of Disinvestment (1999) → NIF (2005) → FIPB abolition (2017) → Air India privatisation (2022). Answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The NIF-DIPAM chronology is the key trap here. DIPAM as a department name is associated with the post-2016 period, but the dedicated Ministry of Disinvestment dates to 1999. Students who associate 'disinvestment proceeds management' with DIPAM may place NIF's creation after DIPAM's establishment, when in fact NIF was created in 2005 and DIPAM (as a restructured department) came later. The FIPB abolition date (2017) is also frequently confused with 2016 or 2015.
solution.final_explanation:
India's disinvestment policy has evolved through distinct institutional phases over two decades.

Correct sequence:
1. Ministry of Disinvestment (1999) — Vajpayee government created a dedicated ministry, signalling policy commitment to disinvestment.
2. National Investment Fund (2005) — UPA government created NIF to receive and deploy disinvestment proceeds for social sector and PSU capital investment.
3. FIPB Abolition (May 2017) — Modi government abolished the Foreign Investment Promotion Board, moving government-route FDI approvals to sectoral ministries.
4. Air India privatisation (January 2022) — Tata Sons acquired Air India, completing India's highest-profile strategic disinvestment.

Wrong options fail by placing NIF before 1999 or missequencing the FIPB abolition and Air India events.

Value Addition:
• The Ministry of Disinvestment was later converted into the Department of Disinvestment and then renamed DIPAM (Department of Investment and Public Asset Management) in 2016.
• Air India's debt was transferred to Air India Asset Holding Limited (AIAHL) before privatisation.
• FIPB's functions were distributed to respective ministries; DPIIT coordinates FDI policy.

solution.concept_anchor: NIMZs — greenfield self-governing industrial townships under NMP 2011
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because PLI is widely associated with Make in India and manufacturing growth — students may accept 'PLI introduced under NMP 2011' as true without knowing PLI came from the 2020 Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative.
elimination_logic: Option (a): NIMZs as 'greenfield, self-governing integrated industrial townships' under NMP 2011 — this is the precise characterisation. Correctly matched.
Option (b): PLI scheme 'introduced under NMP 2011' — PLI was announced in 2020 under Atmanirbhar Bharat, not under NMP 2011. NMP's operational tool was NIMZs. Incorrectly matched.
Option (c): NMP 2011 target of 25% manufacturing GDP share and 100 million jobs by 2022 — these are the correct NMP targets. Correctly matched.
Option (d): Make in India launched in 2014 with 25 focus sectors — this is accurate. Correctly matched.

Option (b) is the NOT correctly matched pair — answer is (a) which is correctly matched (the stem asks which IS correctly matched and only one is definitionally precise; all but (b) are correct, but (b) contains the fabrication).
solution.final_explanation:
NMP 2011 and Make in India are frequently paired in questions, and the PLI-NMP conflation is a common source of error.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: NIMZs (National Investment and Manufacturing Zones) are the flagship operational mechanism of NMP 2011. They are conceived as greenfield, integrated industrial townships with self-governance structures, distinct from SEZs in scale and purpose.
• Option (b) — NOT correctly matched: PLI was NOT introduced under NMP 2011. PLI was announced in 2020 as part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative, administered sector-by-sector by respective ministries. NMP 2011's mechanism was NIMZs, not PLI.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: NMP 2011 set targets of raising manufacturing's GDP share to 25% and creating 100 million additional jobs by 2022 — both were aspirational targets that were not met.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: Make in India was launched on September 25, 2014, with 25 focus sectors for promoting domestic manufacturing and investment.

Value Addition:
• NIMZs are envisioned to be at least 5,000 hectares — far larger than typical SEZs.
• NICDC (National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation) implements industrial corridor projects that are distinct from NIMZs.
• India's manufacturing share in GDP has remained around 16–17%, well below the 25% NMP target.

solution.concept_anchor: Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna investment autonomy levels
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know the broad hierarchy (Maharatna > Navratna > Miniratna) may place the ₹5,000 crore threshold with Maharatna correctly but swap the ₹1,000 crore and ₹500 crore between Navratna and Miniratna I.
elimination_logic: Maharatna PSUs can invest up to ₹5,000 crore or 15% of net worth per project — this is the highest tier. This anchors A-2.
Navratna PSUs have investment autonomy up to ₹1,000 crore without government approval. This anchors B-4.
Miniratna Category I: investment autonomy up to ₹500 crore. This anchors C-3.
Miniratna Category II: investment autonomy up to ₹300 crore — the lowest tier. This anchors D-1. Correct matching is A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1. Answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Navratna vs. Miniratna I investment ceiling swap is a precision trap. Both are real figures (₹1,000 crore and ₹500 crore) that belong to clearly different tiers, but students who haven't memorised the exact allocation may swap them. The key anchor is that Maharatna's ₹5,000 crore (or 15% net worth) is the most distinctive figure — once that is confirmed, the remaining three must be placed in descending order (₹1,000 → ₹500 → ₹300).
solution.final_explanation:
The Ratna framework grants PSUs graduated investment decision-making autonomy without requiring case-by-case government approval.

Correct matches:
• A (Maharatna) — 2: Can invest up to ₹5,000 crore per project, or 15% of net worth, whichever is less — the highest autonomy level.
• B (Navratna) — 4: Can invest up to ₹1,000 crore per project without government approval.
• C (Miniratna Category I) — 3: Investment autonomy up to ₹500 crore per project.
• D (Miniratna Category II) — 1: Investment autonomy up to ₹300 crore per project — the most limited among the four.

Descending order: Maharatna (₹5,000 cr / 15%) > Navratna (₹1,000 cr) > Miniratna I (₹500 cr) > Miniratna II (₹300 cr).

Value Addition:
• Maharatna eligibility also requires turnover ≥ ₹25,000 crore OR net worth ≥ ₹15,000 crore.
• Navratna requires first being a Miniratna Category I and Schedule 'A' CPSE with a composite score of 60/100.
• NTPC, ONGC, Coal India, SAIL are among current Maharatna PSUs.

solution.concept_anchor: Ministry of Cooperation 2021 — rationale and constitutional mandate
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students know the 97th Amendment provided constitutional status to cooperatives and the Ministry of Cooperation was established subsequently — the sequential relationship looks causal but the Ministry was created for operational/political reasons, not as a constitutional requirement.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. A dedicated Ministry of Cooperation was established in July 2021, marking the first time cooperatives had a dedicated central ministry as opposed to being handled by the Department of Agriculture Cooperation.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. The 97th Constitutional Amendment (2011) did NOT mandate the creation of a Ministry of Cooperation. Article 43B (DPSP) directs the state to promote cooperative societies, but a DPSP is not enforceable and does not constitutionally require a dedicated ministry to be created.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect (97th Amendment did not mandate a separate ministry), the answer is (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The causal relationship trap here exploits students who know two true facts (97th Amendment elevated cooperatives constitutionally; Ministry of Cooperation was created in 2021) and construct a causal link. The Amendment provided constitutional recognition but did not mandate a separate ministry — the Ministry was a political and policy choice by the government. Article 43B is a DPSP, which is non-justiciable and cannot compel the creation of a ministry. Treating this sequential relationship as a constitutional mandate is the reversed-causation error.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ministry of Cooperation's creation in 2021 and the 97th Constitutional Amendment are temporally proximate events in cooperative sector governance, but one does not constitutionally mandate the other.

• Assertion (A): Correct. The Ministry of Cooperation was established in July 2021 — the first dedicated central ministry for the cooperative sector, signalling a policy priority shift. Previously, cooperatives were under the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation.
• Reason (R): Incorrect. The 97th Constitutional Amendment (2011) inserted Article 43B as a DPSP (Directive Principle of State Policy) directing the state to promote voluntary formation of cooperatives. DPSPs are non-justiciable — they cannot be enforced in court and certainly do not mandate the creation of a specific ministry. The decision to create the Ministry of Cooperation was a policy decision of the government, not a constitutional obligation arising from the 97th Amendment.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Article 43B (DPSP): 'The State shall endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of cooperative societies.'
• The Ministry of Cooperation's mandate includes revitalising the cooperative sector, especially in rural areas.
• Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT) contains operational provisions for cooperative societies — distinct from Article 43B's aspirational directive.

solution.concept_anchor: FDI prohibited sectors — exact list

statement_analysis.statement: FDI is completely prohibited in the lottery business (including government lotteries, online lotteries) and gambling/betting activities.
statement_analysis.reason: Both categories figure on the FDI prohibited list under India's Consolidated FDI Policy — no FDI is permitted regardless of sector or ownership structure.

statement_analysis.statement: Real estate business is on the FDI prohibited list, and this prohibition extends to construction development projects including townships and housing.
statement_analysis.reason: Only 'real estate business' (buying and selling of completed properties, broking) is prohibited — FDI in construction development (townships, housing, built-up infrastructure) is permitted up to 100% under the automatic route.

statement_analysis.statement: FDI in tobacco manufacturing (cigarettes, cigars, cheroots, and tobacco substitutes) is prohibited in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Tobacco manufacturing is explicitly on the FDI prohibited list under India's Consolidated FDI Policy.

statement_analysis.statement: Chit fund businesses and Nidhi companies are on the FDI prohibited list.
statement_analysis.reason: Both chit funds and Nidhi companies appear explicitly in the list of prohibited sectors for FDI under India's Consolidated FDI Policy.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may correctly identify 3 prohibited sectors but may not know the construction-vs-real estate distinction, accepting Statement 2 as correct and choosing 'All four'.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Lottery and gambling — correctly on the prohibited FDI list. Correct.
Statement 2: Real estate BUSINESS is prohibited but construction DEVELOPMENT is not — the statement extends the prohibition to construction, making it incorrect.
Statement 3: Tobacco manufacturing — correctly prohibited. Correct.
Statement 4: Chit funds and Nidhi companies — both correctly on the prohibited list. Correct.
Three of four are correct (Statements 1, 3, and 4) — answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The real estate vs. construction distinction is one of the most tested partial-truth traps in FDI policy questions. Students know 'real estate' is on the prohibited list and extend this prohibition to all real estate-related activities including construction. The Indian FDI policy makes a precise distinction: 'real estate business' (dealing in completed properties, brokerage) is prohibited, while 'construction development' (building townships, housing, commercial premises) is permitted at 100% FDI. This distinction serves an important policy purpose — India wants FDI in creating new real estate assets, not in speculation on existing ones.
solution.final_explanation:
India's FDI prohibited list is precise and frequently tested for its exact inclusions and the nuanced exclusions within broadly-stated categories.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Lottery (including government/online), gambling, and betting are fully prohibited sectors.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Only 'real estate business' (buying/selling completed property, brokerage, time-sharing) is prohibited. FDI in construction development — building townships, housing projects, commercial real estate — is permitted at 100% under the automatic route. The statement incorrectly extends the prohibition to construction.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Manufacturing of cigars, cigarettes, cheroots, cigarillos, bidis, and tobacco substitutes is prohibited.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Chit funds and Nidhi companies are both on the prohibited list — these are financial entities with regulatory concerns about transparency.

Three statements correct — answer is (c) Only three.

Value Addition:
• FDI is also prohibited in: activities/sectors not open to private sector investment (e.g., atomic energy), and multi-brand retail in states that haven't permitted it (administrative restriction).
• The Consolidated FDI Policy is updated periodically by DPIIT.
• Competition Commission of India (CCI) must approve combinations (mergers/acquisitions) above specified asset/turnover thresholds regardless of FDI route.

solution.concept_anchor: Market failure — natural monopoly justification for public sector
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because the 'commanding heights' doctrine is associated with the same historical period as natural monopoly arguments for public sector, and students may conflate them.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a service with high fixed costs, economies of scale, and social necessity — this is the textbook natural monopoly argument.
Eliminate (a) social equity: equity arguments focus on distributional access across income groups, not on the structural cost characteristics of the service.

Eliminate (b) commanding heights: Nehru's doctrine was a political economy argument about which sectors the state must control strategically — it is broader than the cost-structure rationale in the scenario.

Eliminate (c) capital inadequacy: while private capital inadequacy was a 1950s argument for state intervention, it does not explain the ongoing rationale in the scenario where the cost structure (not capital shortage) is the driver.
Option (d) natural monopoly — high fixed costs, economies of scale, unviability of parallel networks — is the precise economic rationale described. Answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'commanding heights' vs. 'natural monopoly' conflation is common because both have been used to justify public sector ownership of the same industries (electricity, railways). The key distinguishing feature is the logical basis: 'commanding heights' is a strategic/political argument (the state must control the levers of economic power), while 'natural monopoly' is an economic/cost-structure argument (duplicating infrastructure is wasteful because fixed costs are so high). The scenario explicitly references cost structure and scale economies — pointing unambiguously to natural monopoly.
solution.final_explanation:
Multiple economic justifications have been advanced for public sector presence in different industries. The scenario's specific features determine which justification applies.

Scenario analysis: An electricity distribution network requires massive upfront investment in poles, wires, and substations. Once built, the marginal cost of adding a consumer is low, but duplicating the network for competition would be wasteful and uneconomic. This is the classic natural monopoly structure.

• Option (a) — Social equity: The equity argument is about ensuring affordable access to marginalised groups — it doesn't explain why private provision is structurally undesirable. Eliminated.
• Option (b) — Commanding heights: Nehru's doctrine identified certain sectors as strategic for overall economic direction — it was a policy choice, not an economic necessity derived from cost structure. Eliminated.
• Option (c) — Private capital inadequacy: This 1950s argument held that Indian private capital was insufficient for large-scale investment. It doesn't apply where the issue is cost structure rather than capital availability. Eliminated.
• Option (d) — Natural monopoly: Correct. The combination of high fixed costs, decreasing average costs with scale, and the physical network structure that makes duplication inefficient defines a natural monopoly. This is the economic rationale that most precisely explains the scenario.

Value Addition:
• Contestable market theory (Baumol) challenged natural monopoly arguments by showing that potential competition can discipline even single firms.
• Telecom was once a natural monopoly argument sector; technological change enabled competition and privatisation.
• Regulatory bodies like CERC (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission) manage natural monopoly industries where private provision is permitted.

solution.concept_anchor: NCLT jurisdiction; Narsimham Committee bank privatisation recommendations

statement_analysis.statement: The Narsimham Committee on Banking Sector Reforms (1998) recommended reducing government shareholding in public sector banks to below 33% to provide operational autonomy.
statement_analysis.reason: The Narsimham Committee II (1998) recommended reducing government equity in PSBs to 33%, and the first committee (1991) had already recommended a reduction to 51% — the 1998 recommendation was more radical.

statement_analysis.statement: Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks, licensed by RBI, are classified as public sector banks because they serve public purposes mandated by the regulator.
statement_analysis.reason: Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks are private sector entities licensed by RBI — the 'public purpose' of their mandate does not make them public sector banks; they are privately owned and managed.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016, the adjudication of insolvency matters for financial service providers like banks is handled differently from regular companies — the RBI is the designated insolvency regulator for banks.
statement_analysis.reason: IBC provides a different mechanism for financial service providers (FSPs), including banks and insurance companies — these are not subject to the standard CIRP; the respective financial regulator (RBI for banks) plays a key role in the insolvency process.

elimination_logic: Statement 1: Narsimham Committee II (1998) did recommend reducing PSB government equity to 33%. Correct.
Statement 2: Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks are RBI-licensed private sector entities — not public sector. 'Public purpose mandate' does not determine sector classification. Incorrect.
Statement 3: IBC does provide a different insolvency framework for financial service providers (FSPs); the respective financial regulator acts as the designated authority — this is accurate. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the public purpose vs. public ownership confusion. Small Finance Banks serve financially excluded populations (public purpose) and operate under strict RBI conditions — but they are privately owned, not government entities. The entity-swap trap makes students associate 'public purpose licence' with 'public sector'. This is analogous to confusing KVIC (statutory body) with a PSU — the legal character and ownership, not the purpose, determine sector classification.
solution.final_explanation:
Banking sector classification requires careful attention to ownership structure rather than regulatory mandate or purpose.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Narsimham Committee II (1998) went further than its 1991 predecessor, recommending government equity in PSBs be reduced to as low as 33%. The government has not implemented this recommendation, choosing instead selective privatisation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Small Finance Banks (SFBs) and Payment Banks are private sector institutions. RBI licences them and mandates their service orientation (serving small borrowers, enabling digital payments) but this public mandate does not alter their private ownership character. Jan Dhan accounts are facilitated through PSBs and private banks alike.
• Statement 3 — Correct: IBC 2016 treats financial service providers differently. The standard CIRP process under NCLT is modified for banks and insurance companies — the respective financial regulator (RBI, IRDAI) is consulted and plays a designated role.

Value Addition:
• Currently there are 12 PSBs after consolidation; IDBI Bank privatisation (with LIC stake) is pending.
• SFBs include AU Small Finance Bank, Equitas, Jana Bank — all privately owned.
• Scheduled Commercial Banks are classified as: PSBs, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, Small Finance Banks, and Payment Banks.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Consider the following statements about India's banking sector structure and related insolvency framework:

1. The Narsimham Committee on Banking Sector Reforms (1998) recommended reducing government shareholding in public sector banks to below 33% to provide operational autonomy.
2. Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks, licensed by RBI, are classified as public sector banks because they serve public purposes mandated by the regulator.
3. Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016, the adjudication of insolvency matters for financial service providers like banks is handled differently from regular companies — the RBI is the designated insolvency regulator for banks.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 2 and 3 only
(b) 1 and 2 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
